'''Konpira [[Gongen]]''' (金毘羅権現) is a Japanese god of the [[Shugendō]] sect originating in the mountain [[:en:Kotohira|Kotohira]] of {{ill|Kagawa Prefecture|en|Kagawa Prefecture|qid=Q161454|lt=Kagawa Prefecture}}. He is the god of merchant sailors. He is worshipped at {{ill|Kotohira shrines|ja|金刀比羅神社|lt=Kotohira Shrines}}

According to legend {{ill|Konpira Gongen|simple|Konpira Gongen}} came into existence when a priest at {{ill|Matsuo-ji|ja|松尾寺 (香川県琴平町)|qid=Q11529610|lt=Matsuo Temple}} summoned the Ganges deity {{ill|Kumbhīra|ja|宮比羅}}.<ref>https://www.researchgate.net/publication/334586970_Kagawa_A_Guide_to_Sanuki_Gateway_to_Shikoku</ref>

{{ill|Kumbhīra|ja|宮比羅}} was said to have been present at the preaching of the Mahāsamaya Sutta.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kumbhīra |url=https://www.palikanon.com/english/pali_names/ku/kumbhiira.htm |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=www.palikanon.com}}</ref> He is a Ganges crocodile god.<ref>{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2013-06-01 |title=Hinduism 2): Kompira |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2013/06/01/hindu-connections-2-kompira/ |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref>

He is identified with the first of the twelve spirit messengers emanating from {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|Bhaisajyaguru|qid=Q854773|lt=Bhaisajyaguru}}.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=FAURE |first=BERNARD |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/j.ctv1k3np30 |title=Rage and Ravage |date=2021-12-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-8936-4 |doi=10.2307/j.ctv1k3np30}}</ref>{{rp|52}}

Alongside many other water deities like {{ill|Watatsumi|en|Watatsumi|qid=Q1474187|lt=Watatsumi}}, [[Sumiyoshi-taisha|Sumiyoshi]], [[Munakata-sanjojin]], {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|ar|إبيسو (إله)|ca|Ebisu|de|Ebisu|es|Ebisu (mitología)|fa|ابیسو|fi|Ebisu|fr|Ebisu (divinité)|he|אביסו (מיתולוגיה)|id|Ebisu (mitologi)|it|Ebisu (divinità)|ja|えびす|jv|Ebisu (mitologi)|ko|에비스 (신화)|lb|Ebisu (Mythologie)|mni|ꯑꯦꯕꯤꯁꯨ (ꯂꯥꯢ)|nl|Ebisu (god)|pl|Ebisu|ru|Эбису|simple|Ebisu|sv|Ebisu (gud)|th|เอบิซุ (เทพปกรณัม)|tr|Hiru-Ko|uk|Ебісу|vi|Ebisu|zh|惠比寿|qid=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu}}, and [[Gozu Tennō]] his cult became very significant in medieval times.<ref name=":0" />{{rp|316}}

==Overview==
[[Yoshida Kanetomo]] said that Susanoo, the Shinto god of sea and storms, is the same as the Indian god Khumbīra. This god watches over Vulture Peak, a place in {{ill|Buddhist mythology|ar|أساطير بوذية|as|বৌদ্ধ শ্ৰুতিকথা|bn|বৌদ্ধ পুরাণ|ca|Mitologia budista|es|Mitología budista|et|Budistlik mütoloogia|lt|Budistų mitologija|ru|Буддийская мифология|sr|Budistička mitologija|uk|Буддійська міфологія|qid=Q2628860|lt=Buddhist mythology}}...<ref name=":0" />{{rp|172}}

As time passed, people in Japan began to see Konpira as a guardian of their Buddhist religion. They placed Konpira in a shrine on Zōzusan mountain in [[Shikoku]]. This mountain was very important for Shugendō followers by the end of the Heian period. Shugendō is a Japanese belief that combines mountain living, Shinto, and Buddhism. On this mountain, Konpira was given a new name, Konpira Gongen...<ref name=":0" />{{rp|172}}

=== Associations ===
Konpira is connected to gods of water, like dragons and nāga kings. These connections make him a protector of people at sea and the paths they take over the water. This is especially true for the waters inside Japan's coast. In a special part of Buddhism, people honor Konpira as one of twelve powerful spirit leaders. These leaders are linked to twelve directions and twelve animals from the Chinese calendar. Different stories match Konpira to different directions. But most often, he is linked to the north...<ref name=":0" />{{rp|172}}

Sometimes Konpira is identified with gods like Ōkuninushi or {{ill|Shinra Myōjin|ja|新羅明神|ko|신라묘진|qid=Q22127349|lt=Shinra Myōjin}}. ...<ref name=":0" />{{rp|172}} But the most recent identification is with [[Ōmononushi]]. His identification with [[Ōmononushi]] may seem strange at first since [[Ōmononushi]] is a deity of mountains and snakes, while he is a water and navigatonal deity, but the logic behind it is that mountains are often used for navigation in the sea, so mountain deities help sailors..<ref name=":0" />{{rp|317}}

=== In Literature ===
A Buddhist text "[[Sange yōryakki]]" talks about Buddha placing twelve gods on Eagle Peak. One of these gods is Konpira. Here, Konpira is seen as a very important god in Japan. He is thought to be the divine child of Susanoo no Mikoto. People believed that a monk named Saichō came back safely from China because he prayed to Susanoo...<ref name=":0" />{{rp|172}}

In later books, like "Jindai no maki kaden kikigaki" by Koretari, there are more stories. They say Susanoo visited not just Japan but also China and India. These stories suggest that the Japanese gods could be versions of Indian gods. This idea turns the usual story around, with Japanese gods being seen in other countries' stories...<ref name=":0" />{{rp|172}}

==Kotohira Shrines==

{{ill|Kotohira shrines|ja|金刀比羅神社|simple|Kotohira shrines|qid=Q11646488|lt=Kotohira Shrines}} are a kind of {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} in Japan. They were originally dedicated to the syncretic deity [[Konpira Gongen]], but in the Meiji restorration due to [[Shinbutsu bunri]] they were dedicated to [[Ōmononushi]]. Their head shrine is [[Kotohira-gū]]..<ref>{{Cite web |last=SHIKOKU |first=Organization for Promotion of Tourism in |title=Kotohira-gu Shrine |url=https://shikoku-tourism.com/en/see-and-do/10078 |access-date=2023-09-17 |website=Tourism SHIKOKU |language=ja}}</ref><ref name="konpira-shrine:1">{{Cite web |title=Kompirasan |url=https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e5451.html |access-date=2023-09-18 |website=www.japan-guide.com |language=en}}</ref> They are dedicated to seafaring and protecting sailors.<ref name="konpira-shrine:1" />

They are part of the famous Inahachikonten Shrines (稲八金天神社)  of the [[Shrine Consolidation Policy]] alongside {{ill|Inari shrine|en|Inari shrine|qid=Q514480|lt=Inari shrine}}, [[Hachiman shrine|Hachiman Shrine]], {{ill|Kotohira shrines|ja|金刀比羅神社|simple|Kotohira shrines|qid=Q11646488|lt=Kotohira Shrines}}, and [[Tenmangū|Tenmangu Shrine]].

=== History ===
According to legend {{ill|Konpira Gongen|simple|Konpira Gongen}} came into existence when a priest at {{ill|Matsuo-ji|ja|松尾寺 (香川県琴平町)|qid=Q11529610|lt=Matsuo Temple}} summoned the Ganges deity {{ill|Kumbhīra|ja|宮比羅}}.<ref>https://www.researchgate.net/publication/334586970_Kagawa_A_Guide_to_Sanuki_Gateway_to_Shikoku</ref><ref name="konpira-shrine:2">{{Cite book |last=Faure |first=Bernard |date=2021-12-16 |title=Rage and Ravage |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1515/9780824889364 |doi=10.1515/9780824889364|isbn=978-0-8248-8936-4 |s2cid=245466185 }}</ref>{{rp|172}} styarting as a hostile sea monster the deity was placated and became a god of navigation.<ref name="konpira-shrine:2" />{{rp|353}} The deity is perceived as perhaps being a deification of a sea serpent called a {{ill|Wani (dragon)|en|Wani (dragon)|qid=Q20049265|lt=wani}}.<ref name="konpira-shrine:2" />{{rp|437}}

[[Kotohira-gū]] is located close to and strongly historically associated with {{ill|Matsuo-ji|ja|松尾寺 (香川県琴平町)|qid=Q11529610|lt=Matsuo Temple}}<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kotohira: The Area Around the Kotohira-gu Shrine, Where the Old Townscape Remains to This Day |url=https://www.fun-japan.jp/en/articles/10547 |access-date=2023-10-17 |website=FUN! JAPAN International |language=en}}</ref>

In 1889 due to the [[Meiji Restoration]] the head temple was renamed from Konpira temple to [[:en:Kotohira-gu|Kotohira-gu]]..<ref name="konpira-shrine:2" />{{rp|437}}
